c.v: Washtenaw County is home to about 370,000 people in Ann Arbor, Ypsilanti, Saline, Chelsea, Dexter, Milan, and twenty townships, from Pittsfield and Ypsilanti Township on the urban edge to the farm and lake country of the west and north. In 2024, according to the Michigan State Police, 9,844 crashes were reported in the county; 2,231 people were injured in them, 197 seriously, and 35 were killed. The county’s freeways, the University of Michigan and Eastern Michigan University campuses, a large student and pedestrian population, and the rural roads west of US-23 each shape the injury claims that come out of it.

ATLAW is a personal injury firm based in Dearborn, a short drive east of Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor on I-94. In 13 years the firm has handled more than 10,000 cases for injured people in southeast Michigan and recovered more than $100 million for them. This page explains what is particular about a Washtenaw County claim: where the injuries happen, which agencies and institutions are usually on the other side, which courts in Ann Arbor hear the cases, and the deadlines that apply. The practice-area pages linked throughout explain the law for each kind of case.

Its death rate per crash is nearly twice Oakland County’s and close to the state’s, which fits a county where much of the mileage is on high-speed freeways and two-lane rural roads rather than city streets.

I-94 runs east to west through Ypsilanti, the south side of Ann Arbor, and on toward Chelsea and Jackson; US-23 runs north to south along Ann Arbor’s east side; M-14 connects Ann Arbor to Plymouth and I-275. The I-94/US-23 interchange, the US-23/M-14 interchange, and the I-94 interchanges at Ypsilanti carry commuter and freight traffic at speed; freeway crashes there are rear-end, lane-change, and truck crashes, and work-zone crashes during the recurring reconstruction of both freeways. The county recorded 100 pedestrian crashes and 91 bicycle crashes in 2024. A pedestrian or cyclist hit by a car has a no-fault claim even without a car of their own, through a policy in their household or, if there is none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3114(1), 500.3115, 500.3172). The rural roads and the deer.

West and north of Ann Arbor, the county’s roads are two-lane, often unlit, and crossed by deer. Washtenaw recorded 1,409 deer crashes in 2024, more than its pedestrian, bicycle, and motorcycle crashes combined. A deer crash with no other vehicle is a no-fault claim against your own insurer for your injuries; your car is covered only by comprehensive coverage; and a motorcyclist who hits a deer has no PIP claim at all because no motor vehicle was involved. When a driver swerved to avoid a deer and hit another car, the case is about fault like any other crash.
Rental housing, apartments, and student housing.

Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti have large rental markets, many of them student houses and older buildings. Falls on broken stairs and porches, fire and carbon monoxide injuries, and tenant injuries under MCL 554.139 are recurring claims. See our
Two Level I trauma centers serve the county, which means the most seriously injured people in the region are often treated here, and so are many medical malpractice claims. See below.

sections.heading: What is different about a Washtenaw County claim

c.v: The Washtenaw County Road Commission maintains the county roads, including nearly every road in the twenty townships; townships do not own public roads. MDOT owns the state trunklines, including I-94, US-23, M-14, Michigan Avenue (US-12 and Business US-12), and Washtenaw Avenue (M-17 east of US-23; Business Loop I-94 and Business US-23 west of it). The cities, including Ann Arbor, Ypsilanti, Saline, Chelsea, Dexter, and Milan, own their own streets. A road-defect claim against the Road Commission or a city takes written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1402, 691.1404); a road-defect claim against MDOT goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404). In a township, the township itself, not the Road Commission, must keep the public sidewalks in repair (MCL 691.1401(d), 691.1402a).

The University of Michigan and Eastern Michigan University are constitutional state institutions. A claim against either one, including a crash with a university bus or vehicle, an injury caused by a defective university building, or a malpractice claim against the university’s hospital, is a claim against the State: it is filed in the Michigan Court of Claims, tried to a judge without a jury, and requires written notice within six months of the injury under MCL 600.6431, or within 120 days for a defective building (MCL 691.1406). The universities’ own police and campus facilities are part of the same analysis. A claim against a private landlord, a bar, or another driver near campus is an ordinary claim in the ordinary courts.

University of Michigan Health in Ann Arbor is a Level I trauma center for adults and children, and Trinity Health Ann Arbor (formerly St. Joseph Mercy Ann Arbor), in Superior Township, is a Level I trauma center as well. Governmental immunity does not bar a malpractice claim for medical care at a university hospital (MCL 691.1407(4)), but a claim against the University of Michigan’s hospital proceeds against the State in the Court of Claims, while a claim against Trinity Health Ann Arbor proceeds in the circuit court like any private hospital. Both follow Michigan’s malpractice rules: a 182-day Notice of Intent (MCL 600.2912b), an Affidavit of Merit (MCL 600.2912d), a two-year period (MCL 600.5805(8)), and the 2026 noneconomic damages caps of $596,400 and $1,065,000 (MCL 600.1483). TheRide (the Ann Arbor Area Transportation Authority) runs the county’s fixed-route buses; the University of Michigan and Eastern Michigan run campus buses. A crash with a TheRide bus proceeds under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405); a crash with a university bus is a Court of Claims case. A passenger hurt on a bus has a no-fault claim, with priority set by MCL 500.3114(2). See our

Washtenaw County recorded 276 alcohol-involved crashes in 2024. A bar or restaurant that served a visibly intoxicated person or a minor who then caused a crash can be liable under the dram shop act, with written notice within 120 days after the injured person hires a lawyer and suit within two years (MCL 436.1801). faqs.question: How many car accidents happen in Washtenaw County?

answer.v: 9,844 in 2024, according to the Michigan State Police, with 2,231 people injured and 35 killed. Ann Arbor had the most crashes of any community, 2,770.

faqs.question: I was hurt in a crash with a University of Michigan bus. Who do I claim against?

answer.v: The University, which is a state institution, so the claim is filed in the Michigan Court of Claims and tried to a judge, and written notice must be filed within six months for an injury. Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical bills regardless of fault. If no policy in your household covers you, a passenger on the bus claims from the bus’s insurer, and a driver or pedestrian follows the ordinary priority rules.

faqs.question: Can I sue the University of Michigan hospital for malpractice?

answer.v: Yes. Governmental immunity does not bar malpractice claims for medical care at a university hospital, but the claim proceeds against the State in the Court of Claims, with Michigan’s malpractice notice, affidavit, deadline, and cap rules. A claim against a private hospital such as Trinity Health Ann Arbor goes to the circuit court.

faqs.question: I hit a deer. Does insurance pay?

answer.v: Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical bills and lost wages; your comprehensive coverage, if you have it, pays for the car. There is usually no one to sue. A motorcyclist who hits a deer has no PIP claim, because no motor vehicle was involved.

faqs.question: I was hit while walking on campus and I don’t own a car. Who pays my bills?

answer.v: A policy in your household if there is one, including a parent’s policy if you live with them; if not, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan. Students who live away from home should check whether a parent’s policy still covers them.

faqs.question: Who do I notify about a pothole on a township road?

answer.v: The Washtenaw County Road Commission, in writing within 120 days, because townships do not own roads. MDOT, with notice filed with the Court of Claims within 120 days.

answer.v: Our office is at 3 Parklane Boulevard in Dearborn, east of Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor. We welcome clients to our Dearborn office for a consultation. If you are unable to visit, home or hospital visits can be arranged as needed.
